# Show HN draft

<!-- BEGIN facts -->
**Numbers you can quote** (generated by `scripts/update_readme.py` from real runs):

- Rules: 55 (26 CRITICAL/BLOCK, 21 HIGH/WARN, 8 report-only).
- 1189 tests run by default, plus 7 opt-in live-RPC tests that are skipped unless `TXWARDEN_LIVE_RPC` is set.
- Synthetic labelled evals: 2660 cases in 92 categories; accuracy 0.977 (dev 0.977, held-out 0.976); BLOCK precision 0.988, recall 0.970.
- Disagreements with the labels: 14 unsafe ALLOW and 12 over-BLOCK, of which 0 and 0 outside the deliberately ambiguous `gray_area` group. Categories with any miss: `swap_impact_band`, `swap_loose`, `swap_mid_trade_slippage_band`, `swap_slippage_band`.
- The original 122-case set still scores 0.984.
- Prompt-injection eval (a scripted model that obeys every injected instruction): 245 runs, verdict weaker than the engine's in 0, changed after `assess_risk` in 0; 50 runs ended in a fail-closed BLOCK. No real language model was run.
- Not verified: any run against a real Ethereum node, real-world detection rates.

## First comment (post immediately after submitting)

Hi HN, I built TxWarden because most wallet "simulation" demos stop at showing you a balance change,
and the interesting failures are elsewhere: an unlimited approval to a fresh contract, a
`setApprovalForAll`, a swap whose output is routed to someone else, a "claim" contract that pulls your
tokens with an allowance you gave months ago.

What it does: decodes the calldata (about 70 selectors, Universal Router commands, multicall),
dry-runs it against a fork over JSON-RPC, prices swaps with the pool math (constant product and
Uniswap V3 with ticks, including a sandwich estimate), and runs 55 rules to produce
ALLOW/WARN/BLOCK. Python, no runtime dependencies.

The part I care about: an optional LLM agent explains the result, but the verdict is computed by
code, and the agent fails closed. I wrote an eval where the scripted "model" obeys every
instruction it finds in calldata, token names, labels and revert reasons; across the attack
scripts in the repo the verdict never changed. That shows the architecture holds, not that a real
model resists injection (I did not run one; an injected model can still force a BLOCK by refusing to
run the engine, which is a denial of service, not a bypass).

What I would like you to know before you try it, because it matters more than the feature list:

- All evals are synthetic and the labels are mine, written next to the rules. Agreement is high
  where I wrote the template and visibly lower in the swap-threshold categories (the README prints
  the tables and says which). There is no real-world detection rate.
- The RPC path has only been run against an in-memory fake chain served over HTTP, never against a
  real node. There is an opt-in live test file I could not run.
- It reviews transactions only: no EIP-712 permit or order signatures.
- Parts of it were written with an AI coding assistant; the test suite, property tests and eval
  harnesses are how I checked it.

The facts block above lists the current numbers. I would most like (1) real labelled transactions
to score it on, (2) someone with a node to run `pytest -m live`, and (3) people telling me which
rule is wrong.
